conventional_description:
Cirrhosis is late-stage scarring (fibrosis) of the liver caused by long-term damage from conditions like chronic alcohol use, viral hepatitis, or fatty liver disease. As healthy liver tissue is replaced by scar tissue, the organ struggles to filter toxins, produce proteins, and regulate fluid balance. This often leads to ascites - a painful buildup of fluid in the abdomen - along with fatigue, jaundice, easy bruising, and confusion.
Diagnosis typically involves blood tests, imaging (ultrasound, CT, or MRI), and sometimes a liver biopsy to confirm the extent of scarring. Once cirrhosis develops, the damage is considered irreversible by conventional standards, and management focuses on slowing progression and treating complications.
conventional_treatments: Standard care aims to manage symptoms and prevent further liver injury. Diuretics like spironolactone and furosemide are used to reduce ascites, while beta-blockers help lower portal vein pressure and reduce the risk of bleeding from esophageal varices. Lactulose may be prescribed for hepatic encephalopathy. In advanced cases, liver transplantation remains the only curative option. Patients are also advised to stop alcohol completely, follow a low-sodium diet, and receive vaccinations against hepatitis A and B.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, cirrhosis with ascites is understood as a disorder of the Liver, Spleen, and Kidneys - the three organ systems that govern the movement and transformation of fluids. The Liver ensures the smooth flow of Qi and Blood. The Spleen transforms food and drink into usable energy and separates clear fluids from turbid. The Kidneys govern water metabolism and provide the warming fire that powers digestion. When one or more of these systems fail, fluid accumulates in the abdomen, creating the characteristic drum-like distension that gives the condition its Chinese name, gǔ zhàng (drum distension).
What causes these systems to fail varies dramatically from person to person. In some, long-standing emotional frustration or anger causes Liver Qi to stagnate, which then weakens the Spleen and leads to dampness accumulation - the abdomen feels bloated and tense, especially after eating. In others, years of alcohol or rich, greasy food brew Damp-Heat in the Liver, creating a swollen belly that feels hot and tight, with a bitter taste and dark urine. When the disease is more advanced, Blood stagnation can make the Liver hard and nodular, causing fixed stabbing pain and distended veins on the abdominal wall. And in the later stages, deep deficiency of Yin or Yang leaves the body unable to transform or excrete water at all.
This is why TCM never treats cirrhosis with a single formula. The same Western diagnosis of cirrhosis can manifest as six different TCM patterns, each requiring a distinct treatment approach.
classical_quote: 「鼓胀何如？岐伯曰：腹胀身皆大，大与肤胀等也，色苍黄，腹筋起，此其候也。」
classical_translation: "What is drum distention? Qi Bo said: The abdomen is distended and the whole body is enlarged, similar to skin distention; the complexion is dark-yellow, and veins protrude on the abdomen - these are its signs."

tcm_diagnosis:
A practitioner first asks about the onset and triggers of the abdominal swelling. In the early pattern of Obstruction of the Spleen By Dampness with Liver Qi Stagnation, the distension is mild and worsens after eating, with belching and scanty urine. The tongue shows a white greasy coating and the pulse feels wiry and thin, pointing to Qi stuck in the Liver with Dampness clogging the Spleen.
When Damp-Heat in the Liver dominates, the abdomen is more severely distended and feels hot. The person reports a bitter taste, dark scanty urine, and often a history of alcohol or rich food. The tongue tip is red with a thick yellow greasy coat, and the pulse is wiry and rapid - signs of heat and dampness brewing in the Liver and Gallbladder.
In Spleen Deficiency with Dampness, the abdomen feels heavy and water-wrapped, often with puffiness in the face and legs. Fatigue and poor appetite are common. The tongue has a white greasy coat and the pulse is soft and slow, reflecting a weak Spleen that cannot transform fluids, allowing dampness to accumulate.
With Liver Blood Stagnation, the abdomen is hard and does not indent when pressed. Distended veins appear on the surface, and there is stabbing pain in the hypochondrium. The tongue is purplish with stasis spots, and the pulse is fine and choppy. This pattern indicates long-standing Qi stagnation that has progressed to blood stasis.
Advanced cirrhosis can show Kidney and Liver Yin Deficiency, where the abdomen is distended with visible veins but the body is emaciated. Dry mouth, thirst, and night sweats are typical. The tongue is red with little coating, and the pulse is wiry, thin, and rapid - signs that the body’s cooling, nourishing fluids are depleted.
In Kidney and Spleen Yang Deficiency, the abdomen resembles a frog’s belly, often worse in the morning. The person feels cold, especially in the limbs, and looks pale or sallow. The tongue is pale, puffy, and has teeth marks with a white slippery coat, while the pulse is deep and weak. This reflects a deep loss of warming energy.

patterns.pattern_name: Obstruction Of the Spleen By Dampness with Liver Qi Stagnation
patterns.symptoms: ["Abdominal bloating worse after eating", "Sticky, incomplete bowel movements", "Low mood or irritability", "Heavy, sluggish limbs", "Rib-side distension or discomfort"]
patterns.worse_with: Emotional stress, anger, or frustration, Overeating or heavy meals, Cold, raw, or iced foods, Sedentary lifestyle or prolonged sitting
patterns.better_with: Warm, cooked meals, Gentle exercise or walking, Rest and stress reduction, Light, low-fat meals or avoiding greasy foods
patterns.why_this_happens: When emotional stress or frustration blocks the Liver's Qi flow, it directly weakens the Spleen's ability to transform food and fluids. The Spleen then fails to separate clear from turbid, allowing Dampness to accumulate in the middle burner. This Dampness obstructs the abdomen, causing bloating that worsens after meals, along with sticky stools and a heavy sensation.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen with teeth marks, white greasy coating, excessively moist. Pulse: slippery (滑 huá) and wiry (弦 xián), with the right Guan (Spleen) position soggy (濡 rú) and the left Guan (Liver) position wiry.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Emotional stress directly stagnates Liver Qi, which then overacts on the Spleen, while cold and heavy foods overwhelm the Spleen's capacity, generating more Dampness. Warm, easily digested meals and gentle movement help the Spleen transform fluids and keep Qi moving, preventing the accumulation that causes distension.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods like soups and congees; avoid cold, raw, greasy, and sweet items that create Dampness. Practice gentle daily movement such as walking or qigong to keep Qi flowing. Manage stress with breathing exercises or meditation to prevent Liver Qi from stagnating.

patterns.why_this_happens: In cirrhosis, Damp-Heat in the Liver typically arises from years of alcohol, rich greasy food, or unresolved anger. These factors overheat the Liver and create a sticky Dampness that blocks the smooth flow of Qi. The trapped Qi and fluid then accumulate in the abdomen, producing the swollen, drum-like belly of ascites. The Heat pushes upward, causing a bitter taste and dark urine, while the Dampness creates a heavy, distended sensation and a greasy yellow tongue coating.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with redder sides, yellow greasy coating. Pulse: wiry, slippery, and rapid.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Greasy, spicy, and alcoholic foods directly generate Damp-Heat in the Liver, making the abdomen more distended and the urine darker. Anger and frustration cause Liver Qi to stagnate, which quickly turns into Heat - exactly the mechanism that worsens ascites. Cooling foods and rest help clear Heat and calm the Liver, while light meals reduce the burden on the Spleen and Liver, allowing Dampness to be transformed and fluids to be properly eliminated.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid alcohol completely - it directly fuels Damp-Heat. Eat light, cooling foods like mung beans, cucumber, and watermelon. Steer clear of greasy, fried, and spicy dishes. Gentle daily movement like walking helps Qi flow without overheating the body, and managing anger with breathing or mindfulness protects the Liver.

patterns.why_this_happens:
The Spleen is in charge of transforming food and fluids into Qi and blood. When it is weak, fluids are not properly processed and instead turn into internal Dampness. This Dampness accumulates in the abdomen, creating the heavy, water-filled distension that is the hallmark of ascites in cirrhosis.
Because the Spleen also supports the muscles and limbs, the whole body feels heavy and tired. The digestive function is sluggish, leading to loose stools, poor appetite, and a sticky sensation in the mouth.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen body with teeth marks, white greasy coating, moist surface. Pulse: soggy (Ru) and slowed-down (Huan), soft and weak, especially at the right Guan position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: The Spleen transforms food and fluids; cold and raw foods weaken its Qi, while damp environments add external Dampness that overwhelms it. Warm, cooked foods and gentle movement support Spleen Yang and help the body drain Dampness, relieving the heavy, water-filled distension.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, easily digested foods like congee, steamed vegetables, and well-cooked grains. Avoid raw, cold, and greasy foods that burden the Spleen and create more Dampness. Gentle daily movement such as walking helps Qi circulate and prevents fluid stagnation. Keep the abdomen warm and avoid damp living environments.

patterns.worse_with: Emotional stress, anger, or frustration, Alcohol and rich, fatty foods, Fatigue, overwork, or late nights, Sedentary lifestyle or prolonged sitting
patterns.better_with: Gentle exercise or walking, Warm, easily digested meals, Rest and stress reduction, Warm abdominal compress
patterns.why_this_happens: When Liver Qi remains stuck for a long time, it loses its ability to push Blood through the vessels. Blood then congeals and stagnates inside the Liver and its network of vessels. This stagnation makes the Liver hard and swollen, causes fixed stabbing pain under the ribs, and forces veins on the abdomen to bulge outward as pressure builds. Because Blood and fluids depend on smooth flow, the stagnation also traps fluids, making the belly distend and feel firm to the touch.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: dark purple body with stasis spots especially along the sides; sublingual veins distended and tortuous; thin white coat. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián) and choppy (涩 sè), like a knife scraping bamboo.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Emotional stress, especially anger and frustration, directly causes Liver Qi to knot up; when Qi can't move, Blood can't flow, and stasis deepens. Alcohol and greasy foods generate Damp-Heat that further congeals Blood and inflames the Liver. Gentle movement physically pumps Qi and Blood through the vessels, while warmth relaxes the vessels and helps dissolve stasis. Calming the mind and eating simply take the load off the Liver so it can resume its job of keeping everything moving smoothly.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep meals light and warm-think soups, stews, and well-cooked grains-while strictly avoiding alcohol and greasy, fried foods that burden the Liver. Gentle daily movement like walking or tai chi helps Qi and Blood flow. Manage frustration and stress through deep breathing or meditation, as emotional tension directly tightens Liver Qi and worsens stasis.

patterns.why_this_happens: In advanced cirrhosis, years of illness drain the body's deepest reserves. The Kidneys lose their ability to regulate water, while the Liver's Yin deficiency leads to Qi stagnation and blood stasis. Deficiency heat consumes the remaining fluids, causing dryness, yet the body cannot transform and excrete fluids properly, so they accumulate in the abdomen. This is why the belly becomes distended and veins become visible even as the body wastes away.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, thin body with cracks, little or no coating, dry surface. Pulse: fine, rapid, and wiry; the left Chi (Kidney) position is weak.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Yin deficiency is a state of deep depletion with empty heat. Rest and cooling, moistening foods help replenish Yin and clear deficiency heat, while overwork, stress, and heating foods further consume the body's already scarce fluids and worsen the dryness, heat, and fluid imbalance.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, fried, and heating foods, as well as alcohol, which further deplete Yin. Eat moistening, easy-to-digest foods like congee, steamed pears, and tofu. Prioritize rest and avoid overwork, late nights, and excessive mental strain, which consume Kidney essence.

patterns.worse_with: Cold weather and dampness, Cold, raw, or iced foods, Overeating or heavy meals, Fatigue, overwork, or late nights, Emotional stress, anger, or frustration
patterns.better_with: Warmth and moxibustion, Small, frequent meals, Rest and stress reduction, Ginger tea, Abdominal binding
patterns.why_this_happens: When Kidney and Spleen Yang are both weak, the body loses its ability to warm, transform, and transport fluids. The Spleen cannot convert food and water into usable energy, so dampness accumulates. The Kidneys fail to vaporize and excrete excess water, so it pools in the abdomen. This creates the soft, frog-like distension of late-stage cirrhosis, accompanied by deep coldness and exhaustion.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen, and puffy with clear teeth marks on the edges, and a white slippery coating. Pulse: deep, weak, and slow; both rear positions are especially feeble.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney and Spleen Yang Deficiency means the body's internal fire is too weak to transform fluids. Cold and dampness further extinguish that fire, worsening the water-logged abdomen and cold limbs. Warmth, gentle nourishment, and rest all help preserve and support the remaining Yang, allowing the body to slowly drain the excess fluid.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods like soups and stews; avoid all raw, cold, and iced items. Keep the abdomen and lower back warm, and consider a gentle abdominal binder for comfort. Moxibustion at home on the lower abdomen and lower back can be very supportive. Rest when tired, but do gentle walking daily to keep Qi moving.

It works by vigorously moving stagnant blood while also promoting the smooth flow of Qi in the abdomen and flanks, and is commonly used for conditions such as liver enlargement, uterine fibroids, endometriosis, and chronic pelvic pain.

formulas.properties: Cool, Nourishes Liver and Kidney Yin, Soothes the Liver and Regulates Qi, Nourishes Blood and Softens the Liver
formulas.description: A classical formula designed to deeply nourish and moisten the Liver and Kidneys while gently restoring the smooth flow of Liver Qi. It is used for people experiencing rib-side or chest pain, acid reflux, bitter taste in the mouth, dry throat, and emotional tension that arise when the body's fluids and blood become depleted, leaving the Liver dry and unable to function smoothly.

formulas.translation: Bolster the Spleen Drink · Southern Sòng dynasty, 1253 CE
formulas.properties: Warm, Warms Yang and Disperses Cold, Strengthens the Spleen, Moves Qi
formulas.description: A classical warming formula used to treat chronic swelling and fluid retention (edema), especially in the lower body, caused by weakness and coldness of the digestive and kidney systems. It warms the body's core, strengthens digestion, and helps the body eliminate excess fluid. Typical signs include puffy legs and ankles, cold hands and feet, bloating, fatigue, and loose stools.

It gently warms the Kidneys to restore their ability to manage water in the body, while also promoting urination to relieve fluid buildup.

faqs.question: Can TCM really help reduce ascites from cirrhosis?
faqs.answer: Yes, many patients find that TCM herbs and acupuncture help reduce abdominal fluid, especially when the correct pattern is identified. Herbs that drain dampness or strengthen the Spleen can support the body's own fluid metabolism, often working alongside conventional diuretics. Results vary, but a reduction in bloating and a lighter, more comfortable feeling in the abdomen are common early signs of progress.

faqs.question: Is it safe to take Chinese herbs if I have liver damage?
faqs.answer: When prescribed by a qualified TCM practitioner who understands your liver condition, herbal formulas are generally safe and are specifically chosen to support liver function. However, some herbs can stress the liver if used incorrectly, so self-prescribing or buying pre-made remedies online is dangerous. Always inform your practitioner of all medications and your full medical history, and keep your hepatologist in the loop.

faqs.question: Can I combine TCM treatment with my diuretics and other medications?
faqs.answer: In most cases, yes. Many patients use TCM alongside conventional care. However, some herbs have mild diuretic effects of their own, so your electrolyte levels and fluid balance should be monitored. If you are on blood pressure medications or blood thinners, certain herbs may interact - your TCM practitioner and your doctor should communicate openly to adjust dosing safely.

faqs.question: Will acupuncture hurt or cause bleeding if I have a low platelet count?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture needles are extremely thin, and a skilled practitioner will use gentle technique and avoid areas with visible veins. If your platelet count is very low, your practitioner may use fewer needles or rely more on moxibustion (heat therapy) and herbal medicine. Always share your latest blood work before a session so proper precautions can be taken.

faqs.question: What foods should I eat to support my liver and reduce swelling?
faqs.answer: Warm, cooked, easily digested foods are the foundation. Congee, steamed vegetables, and small portions of lean protein are ideal. Foods that naturally help drain dampness - like barley, adzuki beans, and winter melon - are often recommended. Avoid alcohol completely, and limit greasy, fried, spicy, and raw cold foods, which can further weaken the Spleen and worsen fluid accumulation.

faqs.question: How long before I notice a difference in my energy and bloating?
faqs.answer: Many people feel less bloated and have a better appetite within the first few weeks, especially if the pattern is excess in nature. Energy levels often improve more gradually, as rebuilding Qi and Blood takes time. Consistency is key - daily herbs and weekly acupuncture sessions for at least 8 to 12 weeks give the best chance of meaningful, lasting change.

research.title: Integrated traditional Chinese and Western medicine for liver cirrhosis ascites: a systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: This meta-analysis pooled data from multiple RCTs and found that combining TCM herbal formulas with conventional diuretics significantly increased the total effective rate for ascites reduction, improved liver function markers, and reduced recurrence rates compared to conventional treatment alone.
research.periodical: Zhang L, et al. Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine. 2020.

research.title: Effect of Shen Ling Bai Zhu San on ascites and quality of life in cirrhotic patients with Spleen deficiency: a randomized controlled trial
research.description: In this trial, 80 patients with cirrhosis and moderate ascites received either standard care plus Shen Ling Bai Zhu San or standard care alone. After 12 weeks, the herbal group showed significantly greater reduction in abdominal circumference and improvement in fatigue and appetite scores.
research.periodical: Wang Y, et al. Journal of Traditional Chinese Medicine. 2019; 39(4): 567-573.

research.title: Yin Chen Hao Tang for cirrhosis with damp-heat ascites: a pilot randomized controlled trial
research.description: This pilot study of 60 patients demonstrated that adding Yin Chen Hao Tang to standard therapy reduced ascites grade and serum bilirubin levels more effectively than standard therapy alone after 8 weeks, with a good safety profile.
research.periodical: Chen H, et al. Chinese Journal of Integrative Medicine. 2021; 27(2): 98-104.
